# **Stochastic Topologies in Extreme-Edge AI: Bayesian Distillation and Variance-Bounded Markovian Routing on the Hypersimplex for the QMINIWASM 1.58-bit Architecture**

## **Abstract**

The relentless scaling of modern artificial intelligence has encountered a critical physical boundary, often termed the thermodynamic imperative. Traditional continuous floating-point architectures, constrained by von Neumann memory bottlenecks and catastrophic energy dissipation, fundamentally limit the deployment of high-dimensional reasoning models on heavily constrained extreme-edge environments such as WebAssembly (WASM) runtimes. The QMINIWASM architecture represents a radical paradigm shift, completely eradicating continuous floating-point arithmetic in favor of a 1.58-bit ternary quantization lattice (![][image1]) executing via hybrid quantum-classical computing protocols. However, transitioning a neural network from a continuous parameter space to a rigid, discrete topological space typically results in severe capacity collapse and gradient death. This paper provides an exhaustive, deep-dive theoretical analysis of the QMINIWASM Cascade Reinforcement Learning (Cascade RL) training pipeline, which resolves these topological disconnects. By framing the training pipeline as a complex Markov Decision Process (MDP), the analysis elucidates the probabilistic phase transitions required for extreme quantization. It is demonstrated how simulated annealing functions as a Markov chain to freeze continuous sub-graphs into the ternary lattice, and how Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) utilizes synthetic reasoning traces and a reverse-Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence algorithm to perform Bayesian-like posterior updates. Furthermore, the paper rigorously analyzes the geometric routing of the discrete space via Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO). By analyzing the router through the lens of tropical geometry—specifically its algebraic isomorphism to the Normal Fan of a Hypersimplex—the paper details why standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) fails due to token dropout. Ultimately, it is shown how CISPO acts as a variance-bounded, weighted Markovian reward mechanism that ensures uniform exploration of the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) parameter space, thereby preserving the "Combinatorial Resilience" essential for executing advanced artificial intelligence within the austere operational parameters of extreme-edge architectures.

## **1\. Introduction: The Thermodynamic Imperative and Topological Constraints of Edge AI**

The evolution of artificial intelligence over the past decade has historically been predicated on the aggressive scaling of continuous, high-precision parameter spaces.1 The prevailing orthodoxy has relied heavily on 32-bit (FP32) and 16-bit (FP16 or BF16) floating-point arithmetic to capture the complex, highly non-linear topological manifolds required for advanced cognitive reasoning and language modeling. However, the physical realities of computation—governed by Landauer’s principle and the overarching thermodynamic imperative of energy dissipation—dictate that the future of ubiquitous intelligence cannot sustainably rely on standard floating-point operations.3 In environments characterized by extreme constraints, such as internet-of-things (IoT) edge devices and browser-based WebAssembly (WASM) execution runtimes, the energy cost associated with moving continuous data between memory and processing units—the infamous von Neumann bottleneck—vastly eclipses the energy cost of the mathematical computation itself.1

The QMINIWASM architecture directly addresses this fundamental physical limitation by initiating a paradigm shift away from continuous manifolds, moving entirely to a 1.58-bit ternary quantization lattice.1 In this architecture, every weight within the neural network is strictly constrained to the discrete set ![][image1]. This ternary regime, which mathematically encapsulates ![][image2] bits of information per parameter, transforms all dense matrix multiplications into simple, highly efficient addition and subtraction operations, or their bitwise logical equivalents.1 These operations execute with profound thermodynamic efficiency and minimal latency in WASM environments, drastically reducing the memory footprint while maintaining high throughput.2

Furthermore, the QMINIWASM paradigm introduces a novel hybrid quantum-classical computing framework. The ternary lattice of ![][image1] is not merely a classical computational convenience but serves as an isomorphic bridge to ternary quantum logic, specifically mapping to qutrit states.7 By utilizing the qutrit Clifford group, QMINIWASM allows classical WASM runtimes to interface seamlessly with quantum sub-routines, providing a fault-tolerant structural baseline that enhances the expressivity of the discrete model far beyond what classical binary models can achieve.9

While the inference-time advantages of a discrete ternary lattice are immense, the training-time reality presents a profound mathematical and geometric challenge. Neural networks inherently rely on the smooth topology of continuous spaces (![][image3]) to allow gradient-based optimization through backpropagation. Forcing a continuous, highly expressive manifold into a rigid, non-differentiable discrete lattice routinely triggers "catastrophic forgetting," capacity collapse, and gradient death, rendering the network effectively paralyzed.2 Traditional post-training quantization (PTQ) techniques often result in sub-optimal mappings that destroy the intricate reasoning capabilities embedded in the network's continuous topological boundaries.1

To bridge this mathematical chasm, the QMINIWASM framework utilizes a highly specialized, four-phase curriculum known as Cascade Reinforcement Learning (Cascade RL).12 This pipeline does not simply round weights to the nearest integer; instead, it orchestrates a controlled, probabilistic phase transition. By framing the entire training pipeline as a complex Markov Decision Process (MDP), the architecture carefully manages the entropy of the network. The transition from a continuous to a discrete topological space requires advanced variance-bounding and Bayesian updating to preserve cognitive capabilities. This paper will systematically deconstruct how combining Bayesian probability matching with variance-bounded discrete Markovian policy steps enables the QMINIWASM architecture to achieve state-of-the-art reasoning capabilities without violating the thermodynamic limits of the extreme edge.

## **2\. The QMINIWASM Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architecture**

Before examining the probabilistic training pipeline, it is necessary to thoroughly understand the target deployment architecture. The QMINIWASM framework is designed specifically for WebAssembly, a binary instruction format that provides a sandboxed execution environment with near-native performance inside web browsers and edge devices. WebAssembly is fundamentally constrained by its linear memory model and limited instruction set, making traditional continuous tensor operations highly inefficient when scaled to billions of parameters.

### **2.1 The 1.58-Bit Ternary Lattice**

To circumvent the von Neumann memory wall inherent to WASM, QMINIWASM employs extreme quantization. The continuous weight matrices ![][image4] are projected into a ternary state ![][image5]. This quantization completely eliminates the need for floating-point multiplication during the forward pass.2 Instead, the standard linear projection ![][image6] is computed utilizing only signed additions, significantly reducing the computational complexity from ![][image7] floating-point operations to ![][image7] integer additions. This mechanism yields a Pareto-optimal solution that dramatically reduces latency, power consumption, and memory footprint, often achieving a 4$\\times$ reduction in storage requirements.2

### **2.2 Quantum-Classical Isomorphism via Qutrit Clifford Groups**

A defining characteristic of QMINIWASM is its extension beyond classical bitwise optimization into hybrid quantum-classical computing. The ternary states ![][image1] are mathematically analogous to the three orthogonal basis states of a quantum integer, or qutrit, typically denoted as ![][image8].7 In hybrid architectures, the classical ternary lattice can act as a direct simulator or control plane for quantum algorithms operating within the qutrit Clifford group.7

The qutrit Clifford group, generated by the Hadamard, Phase (S), and Controlled-Z (CZ) gates, serves as the backbone for designing fault-tolerant quantum operations.7 The operations within QMINIWASM's classical ternary lattice map directly onto these generators. Consequently, the network's internal representations can be effortlessly serialized and offloaded to quantum processing units (QPUs) for complex, high-dimensional probability sampling, while the deterministic routing and accumulation operations remain in the classical WASM runtime.8 This hybrid synergy allows the discrete model to leverage quantum superposition for probabilistic exploration during training, providing a distinct mathematical advantage over purely classical binary quantization frameworks.

## **3\. Cascade RL as a Non-Stationary Markov Decision Process**

The transition from the continuous pre-training phase to the discrete execution phase is the most perilous stage in extreme-edge model development. Forcing a continuous, highly expressive manifold into a rigid, non-differentiable discrete lattice routinely triggers gradient death.2 To mitigate this, QMINIWASM models the entire post-training quantization pipeline as a non-stationary Markov Decision Process (MDP), utilizing a structured curriculum known as Cascade Reinforcement Learning.13

A standard MDP is defined by the tuple ![][image11], where ![][image12] is the state space, ![][image13] is the action space, ![][image14] defines the transition dynamics, ![][image15] is the reward function, and ![][image16] is the discount factor. In the context of the QMINIWASM Cascade RL pipeline, these components are redefined geometrically and topologically:

* **State Space (![][image12]):** The state represents the current topological configuration of the network's parameters, transitioning from continuous (![][image3]) to discrete (![][image17]).  
* **Action Space (![][image13]):** The set of optimization steps, weight updates, and quantization constraints applied by the policy at each iteration.  
* **Transition Dynamics (![][image14]):** The probabilistic evolution of the network's geometry. Because the nature of the state space fundamentally shifts from continuous to discrete, the transition probabilities are inherently non-stationary.  
* **Reward Function (![][image15]):** The domain-specific signals guiding the alignment of the network, derived from supervised targets, synthetic data, and verifiable outcomes.12

The Cascade RL pipeline decomposes this immense topological shift into four distinct phases, ensuring that the transition probabilities remain stable and that the network's accumulated knowledge is preserved across mathematical boundaries.15

### **3.1 Phase 1: Continuous Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**

The pipeline initiates with Continuous Supervised Fine-Tuning. Operating entirely within the continuous floating-point domain, this phase is responsible for mapping the global topological boundaries of the target tasks.17 By processing massive datasets of high-quality reasoning traces, the network establishes the cognitive priors and foundational decision manifolds.15 While this continuous model cannot be deployed in WASM, it serves as the topological blueprint—the ultimate source of truth—that the subsequent quantization phases must attempt to mimic.

## **4\. The Probabilistic Phase Transition: Simulated Annealing and Markov Chains**

Phase 2 of the QMINIWASM Cascade RL pipeline is Progressive Quantization, marking the precise point where the continuous network first intersects the discrete ternary lattice. Standard quantization-aware training (QAT) mechanisms typically rely on Straight-Through Estimators (STEs) to bypass the non-differentiability of the step function during backpropagation.11 However, in the extreme 1.58-bit regime, STEs suffer from severe quantization noise. The aggressive rounding operations create a massive gradient mismatch between the forward and backward passes, leading to highly unstable training trajectories and ultimately, parameter collapse.11

To counter this geometric destabilization, QMINIWASM models the progressive quantization as a thermodynamic cooling process, heavily utilizing the principles of simulated annealing.19 Rather than forcing an immediate discretization, the network parameters are treated as particles in a complex physical system seeking a state of minimum free energy within a constrained landscape. The transition of a continuous weight ![][image18] to a discrete ternary state ![][image19] is governed by a carefully modulated Markov chain.

### **4.1 Metropolis-Hastings and Thermodynamic Cooling**

In this framework, let ![][image20] represent the energy of the network configuration (analogous to the negative log-likelihood or the loss function), where ![][image21] represents the parameter vector. The probability of the network transitioning from a continuous configuration ![][image22] to a progressively more discrete configuration ![][image23] is defined by the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance criterion:

![][image24]  
Here, ![][image25] represents the computational temperature parameter. At the inception of Phase 2, the temperature ![][image25] is maintained at a high state. This high thermodynamic temperature significantly flattens the transition probability distribution, enabling the continuous weights to freely explore the surrounding topological space and temporarily accept higher-loss, sub-optimal configurations.

This stochastic exploration is mathematically critical; it prevents the network from snapping into suboptimal, localized discrete minima—a primary failure mode that plagues standard post-training quantization techniques.11 By injecting controlled thermal noise into the Markov chain, the algorithm ensures that the continuous parameters sample a wide array of potential lattice intersections before committing to a specific discrete vertex.

As the Markov chain progresses through the training epochs, the temperature ![][image25] is subjected to a predefined exponential decay schedule, typically formulated as ![][image26], where ![][image27] represents the cooling rate. As ![][image28], the exponential term dominates, and the transition probabilities become increasingly deterministic. The continuous weights, having explored the available topological space, are progressively "frozen" into the nearest stable vertices of the ![][image1] ternary lattice.19

This progressive phase transition effectively maps the dense continuous sub-graphs, formulated during Phase 1 (SFT), into sparse, highly structured discrete combinations. The strictly Markovian nature of this process ensures that the transition probability depends solely on the immediate prior state of the network geometry. This lack of historical dependence allows the topology to warp and adapt sequentially to the encroaching ternary constraints without causing a catastrophic disruption to the global reasoning pathways.

## **5\. Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD): Bayesian Probability Matching**

Once the network has been completely mapped to the ternary lattice and the temperature parameter ![][image25] has reached absolute zero, the model enters Phase 3 of the Cascade RL pipeline: Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD).15 Because the progressive quantization inherently degrades some of the highly nuanced continuous reasoning capabilities, the network must undergo a rigorous restorative alignment process.15

However, directly applying standard gradient-based optimization to the newly formed discrete parameters introduces massive variance, often resulting in "capability drift" or the "see-saw" effect, where improving one domain causes catastrophic regressions in another.17 QMINIWASM mitigates this instability by formulating MOPD as a process of Bayesian probability matching, utilizing massive synthetic reasoning traces generated by the continuous precursors of the network.21

### **5.1 The Distillation Architecture and Teacher Pools**

In the MOPD framework, the continuous, full-precision checkpoints saved during Phase 1 (SFT) and the early, high-temperature stages of Phase 2 are utilized as a diverse pool of "domain-specific teachers".13 The fully 1.58-bit quantized model acts as the "student." The fundamental objective of this phase is to forcefully distill the continuous probability mass of the teacher (![][image29]) into the discrete vertices of the student policy (![][image30]).15

Because both the continuous teachers and the discrete student share identical architectures, tokenizers, and vocabularies—differing only in their quantization state—distribution shift is drastically minimized.21 This structural homogeneity allows for highly dense token-level training, providing a significant advantage over traditional RL methods that rely on sparse, delayed outcome rewards.21

### **5.2 Reverse-KL Divergence as a Mode-Seeking Operator**

To execute this alignment, MOPD employs a reverse-Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence formulation.15 The choice of divergence is critical when dealing with discrete topological spaces. The forward-KL divergence, ![][image31], commonly used in standard machine learning, is *mean-seeking*. It heavily penalizes the student for failing to cover the entire broad distribution of the teacher. In a discrete ternary architecture, attempting to cover a wide, continuous distribution is mathematically impossible; the rigid constraints of the ![][image1] lattice cannot smoothly interpolate across the continuous space, leading to severe gradient pathology and gradient death.23

Conversely, the reverse-KL divergence, ![][image32], is inherently *mode-seeking*.23 It penalizes the student for allocating probability mass in regions where the teacher has none, essentially forcing the discrete student to align its limited capacity tightly with the highest-density peaks (the modes) of the teacher's synthesized output distributions.23

### **5.3 Bayesian Interpretation and Posterior Updating**

This reverse-KL formulation possesses a profound Bayesian interpretation.25 In the context of the MDP, the continuous teacher's output distribution ![][image34] serves as a high-confidence likelihood function representing the "ground truth" of the reasoning trace. The student's current discrete policy ![][image35] acts as the prior distribution.25

The reverse-KL divergence measures the information lost when the prior is used to approximate the posterior. By minimizing this divergence, the QMINIWASM pipeline effectively executes a continuous-to-discrete Bayesian update. The model is dynamically updating its internal beliefs (the ternary weights) to maximize the probability of the observed synthetic data (the teacher's output).

This update is applied sequentially at the token level using a distillation advantage function, ![][image36], which directly guides the reinforcement learning optimization 22:

![][image37]  
Intuitively, when the continuous domain teacher assigns a higher probability to a specific reasoning token than the current quantized student policy, the resulting distillation advantage is highly positive.24 This dense, immediate reward signal forcefully pulls the ternary parameters toward the dominant logical modes of the full-precision network. Because the student is continually sampling from its own on-policy rollouts during this phase, it learns to navigate its newly rigid, discrete state space by utilizing the precise cognitive landmarks established by its continuous predecessor. This Bayesian probability matching acts as a stabilization anchor, ensuring that the model retains its complex reasoning capabilities despite the extreme reduction in parameter precision.13

## **6\. Geometric Routing on the Hypersimplex: Tropical Geometry of the MoE**

The final, most mathematically complex stage of the QMINIWASM Cascade RL pipeline is Phase 4: Geometric Routing via Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO). Extreme-edge WASM deployments rely heavily on Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures to achieve massive reasoning capacity while keeping the active parameter counts—and therefore active memory bandwidth and computational latency—strictly constrained.27 However, conditional routing within a ternary lattice requires navigating a radically different topological landscape than routing within a continuous FP32 neural network.

Recent breakthroughs in algebraic geometry have demonstrated that MoE routing mechanisms are not merely heuristic computational shortcuts aimed at improving system efficiency; rather, they are fundamentally rooted in tropical geometry.29

### **6.1 The Tropical Semiring and Top\-![][image38] Routing Isomorphism**

In the tropical semiring ![][image39], standard arithmetic operations are redefined. Tropical addition ![][image40] is defined as the maximum operator (![][image41]), and tropical multiplication ![][image42] is defined as standard addition (![][image43]).30

Within the QMINIWASM MoE architecture, the Top\-![][image38] routing mechanism is used to select the active subset of ternary experts for any given input. Theoretical analysis establishes that this Top\-![][image38] operation is algebraically isomorphic to the ![][image38]\-th elementary symmetric tropical polynomial.27

When evaluating an input vector ![][image44], the routing layer computes logits for ![][image45] available experts. The aggregate score for any specific coalition of experts ![][image46] (where the size of ![][image46] is ![][image38]) is given by ![][image47]. The router's function is to identify the specific coalition that maximizes this sum.30 Through the lens of tropical geometry, this operation geometrically partitions the high-dimensional input space into a series of convex polyhedral cells, creating what is known as an Affine Order\-![][image38] Voronoi Diagram.30

The decision boundaries of the router—the exact mathematical coordinates where the router shifts activation from one coalition of experts to another—correspond perfectly to the singular locus of the tropical polynomial.30 These are the non-differentiable "creases" in the convex function where at least two distinct expert coalitions achieve the exact same maximum aggregate score.30

### **6.2 The Hypersimplex Normal Fan and Combinatorial Resilience**

Critically, this algebraic isomorphism proves that the Top\-![][image38] routing mechanism partitions the input space into the Normal Fan of a ![][image48]\-Hypersimplex (![][image49]).29 This geometric revelation yields a critical theoretical insight utilized extensively by the QMINIWASM framework: *sparsity is combinatorial depth*.27

While traditional dense neural networks scale their geometric capacity polynomially by increasing depth (adding layers) and width (adding neurons), MoE architectures scale their expressivity by the binomial coefficient ![][image50].27

This exponential scaling of expressivity leads directly to the phenomenon of "Combinatorial Resilience".27 In standard dense networks, pushing continuous parameters into a rigid ![][image1] lattice causes severe geometric capacity collapse, particularly on low-dimensional data manifolds.27 The topological folds and decision boundaries simply flatten out, destroying the model's ability to separate complex features.

Conversely, the MoE architecture deployed in QMINIWASM maintains profound expressivity despite extreme ternary quantization. The transversality of the routing cones—the complex, intersecting angles of the Hypersimplex Normal Fan—preserves the highly dense partitioning of the input space.27 In this paradigm, the intelligence of the network is not stored solely within the individual discrete weights of the ternary experts, but rather within the vast combinatorial pathways generated by successfully navigating the tropical geometry of the router itself.

## **7\. CISPO: Variance-Bounded Markovian Routing on the Hypersimplex**

To successfully leverage Combinatorial Resilience and navigate the complex, non-differentiable creases of the Hypersimplex Normal Fan, QMINIWASM requires an exceptionally stable reinforcement learning algorithm. In standard continuous LLM post-training, algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) are the established defaults.32

### **7.1 The Failure of PPO: Token Dropout and Gradient Death**

PPO and GRPO utilize a surrogate objective function that aims to prevent destructively large policy updates by clipping the importance sampling ratio ![][image52] multiplied by the advantage estimate ![][image53].34 The standard PPO formulation is:

![][image54]  
While highly effective in smooth, continuous environments, this standard clipping mechanism fails catastrophically when applied to the discrete, rigid tropical geometry of the QMINIWASM ternary lattice.37 The primary failure mechanism is defined as "gradient suppression of critical tokens," more commonly referred to as token dropout.37

In complex logical reasoning tasks—such as mathematical theorem proving or code generation, which are primary use cases for extreme-edge AI—critical low-probability tokens (e.g., "Wait," "However," "Recheck," or "Aha") serve as crucial inflection points.37 These specific tokens trigger error correction protocols and initiate deeper logical branching. Because they signify a shift in reasoning, these tokens initially possess very low probabilities under the old policy (![][image55]).37

When the reinforcement learning optimization step correctly identifies these tokens as highly advantageous and attempts to increase their likelihood, it results in a massive, instantaneous surge in the importance sampling ratio ![][image56].37 Under PPO or GRPO, this extreme ratio immediately triggers the mathematical clipping mechanism, which subsequently drops the gradient for that specific token to zero to maintain policy proximity.36

In a ternary model, where the decision boundaries are sharp, non-differentiable tropical creases rather than smooth curves, discarding these critical gradient updates causes immediate geometric gradient death.31 The model simply ceases to learn how to navigate the complex inflection points of the Normal Fan, leading to truncated reasoning traces and overall task failure.

### **7.2 The CISPO Objective Function and The Detach Operator**

To resolve this architectural bottleneck, QMINIWASM employs Phase 4: Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO).37 Instead of clipping the combined surrogate objective—which inherently masks the gradient—CISPO exclusively clips the *importance sampling weights themselves*, while strictly preserving the gradient flow for all generated tokens.37

![][image57]  
In this formulation, two critical mathematical mechanisms operate simultaneously to guarantee the stability of the QMINIWASM router:

**1\. Direct Weight Clipping:** The importance sampling weight is directly bounded by the parameter ![][image58]. In contrast to PPO, which typically utilizes a narrow clipping range (e.g., ![][image59]), CISPO utilizes a significantly larger upper threshold (typically ![][image60]).37 By applying the ![][image61] operator directly to the ratio, CISPO tightly bounds the variance of the update, preventing massive mathematical divergence in the batched RL setting without completely neutralizing large, necessary leaps in policy probability.39

**2\. The Detach Operator:** The most profound architectural deviation in CISPO is the application of the detach operation to the clamped importance weights.37 In modern computational graph dynamics (e.g., PyTorch), detaching a tensor explicitly removes it from the autograd computation sequence. Consequently, the clipped importance weights serve strictly as constant scalar coefficients during the optimization step.37 The actual mathematical gradients flowing back into the ternary parameters are derived exclusively from the ![][image62] likelihood term.37

### **7.3 CISPO as a Variance-Bounded Markovian Reward Mechanism**

Because the gradient computation is isolated strictly to the log-probability term, *every single token*—no matter how rare or how extreme its initial importance ratio—contributes an unbiased gradient to the policy update.37 There is no gradient suppression; there is no token dropout.

This continuous, unsuppressed flow of gradients acts as a dynamically weighted Markovian reward mechanism.40 At each discrete timestep in the training iteration, the policy takes a variance-bounded Markovian step across the non-differentiable boundaries of the Hypersimplex Normal Fan. By weighting the gradient of every token by its detached importance and advantage, CISPO ensures a highly uniform exploration of the vast MoE parameter space.

By utilizing CISPO for the final geometric routing phase, QMINIWASM maintains high sample efficiency and remarkably smooth training trajectories. It overcomes the inherent topological brittleness of the 1.58-bit lattice, allowing the model to fully leverage the Combinatorial Resilience generated by its tropical geometry to execute complex chain-of-thought reasoning without suffering from capacity collapse.30

## **8\. Conclusion: Implications for Extreme-Edge WASM Deployment**

The transition toward 1.58-bit artificial intelligence represents both an inevitable thermodynamic necessity and a formidable topological challenge.1 The QMINIWASM architecture definitively resolves the mathematical paradox of achieving high-dimensional, infinite-precision reasoning within a strictly constrained discrete parameter space. By completely eschewing standard post-training quantization techniques in favor of a highly sophisticated Cascade Reinforcement Learning pipeline, QMINIWASM successfully orchestrates a controlled, probabilistic collapse of network entropy.1

The success of this architecture relies fundamentally on its probabilistic mapping mechanisms and non-stationary Markovian design. Simulated annealing operates as a thermodynamic Markov chain, delicately cooling continuous weights into stable ternary vertices, thereby preventing premature gradient death during the initial quantization phase.19 Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) subsequently implements a dense, token-level reverse-KL divergence protocol.15 By executing continuous-to-discrete Bayesian posterior updates, MOPD forces the rigid ternary student policy to precisely match the complex cognitive modes of the full-precision teacher, acting as an anchor against capability drift.

Crucially, QMINIWASM leverages the algebraic isomorphism between Mixture-of-Experts routing and the tropical geometry of the Hypersimplex Normal Fan to ensure Combinatorial Resilience against the extreme quantization bottleneck.29 By implementing Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO), the framework detaches clipped importance weights, isolating gradient flow strictly to the log-probability term. This eliminates the token dropout characteristic of standard Proximal Policy Optimization algorithms, providing a variance-bounded Markovian reward mechanism capable of successfully navigating the non-differentiable creases of the discrete MoE manifold.37

The resulting architecture presents profound implications for the future of extreme-edge computing. In modern WebAssembly environments—such as browsers or heavily constrained IoT embedded hardware—continuous floating-point memory bandwidth is the primary operational bottleneck.1 The 1.58-bit ternary quantization allows QMINIWASM to completely bypass these von Neumann limitations.1 Because the model’s reasoning pathways were heavily reinforced via Bayesian distillation (MOPD) and navigated via variance-bounded routing (CISPO), the discrete operational execution at inference time exhibits minimal degradation in perplexity compared to massive, full-precision models.1

Ultimately, the convergence of Bayesian probability matching, advanced tropical geometric analysis, and variance-bounded discrete Markovian policy optimization allows the QMINIWASM framework to maintain unprecedented intelligence density. It establishes a rigorous, scalable blueprint for deploying sophisticated, reasoning-capable AI models onto the world's most heavily constrained, decentralized WebAssembly and hybrid quantum-classical computing runtimes.
